units.citation: Binam et al. (2015). Effects of farmer managed natural regeneration on livelihoods in semi-arid West Africa. Environmental Economics and Policy Studies.
units.quote:
As indicated in the results reported in Table 5, moving
from low to young FMNR status increases gross income by 10 % in the Sahel.

relationship.outcome_raw: gross household income per capita (incl. valued own consumption), Sahel pooled, moving from low to new/young FMNR practice; pathway per the authors: fuelwood, fodder, fruit, leaves and other products of the regenerated trees used and sold

context.practice_as_described: farmer managed natural regeneration: actively managing and protecting non-planted trees and shrubs on farmland — farmers identify and protect wildlings and stump/root sprouts, keep about five of the strongest stems and prune the rest, periodically harvesting stems for firewood and timber; households classed as low, new/young or continuous FMNR practitioners from tree density by diameter class, species diversity kept, tenure and FMNR knowledge (regeneration index); manure, compost, fertiliser trees, zai and stone bunds are used alongside on many plots

units.citation: Chang et al. (2021). Windbreak efficiency in controlling wind erosion and particulate matter concentrations from farmlands. Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment.
units.quote:
Windbreak patches could control wind erosion by decreasing wind 
speed, resulting in a reduction of soil loss by an average of 20 % 
compared with agricultural wind erosion in our study (Table 2).

relationship.outcome_raw: mean wind-erosion soil loss (sediment traps) under windbreak patches vs open farmland, high-wind events

context.practice_as_described: poplar (Populus simonii) windbreaks around farmlands, built since the 1970s with the Three-North Shelterbelt Program to control wind erosion; 'windbreak patches' (tree blocks 6-14 m tall, 800-2000 trees/ha, located downwind of farmland) and 'windbreak strips' (2-7 rows, 8-17 m tall); shrubs (seabuckthorn, Caragana korshinskii, apricot) also planted against wind erosion; measured in the non-foliage period before disking
context.note: Sediment traps and wind stations, late March-early May 2017, during high wind events (1-min wind > 5 m/s at 2 m); nine windbreak patches vs farmland, plus grassland and shrubland sites. PICOS caveat: soil loss and wind were measured UNDER the windbreak-patch canopy vs open farmland, not on cropland sheltered by a belt; patches are tree blocks, so the linear_boundary family tag needs a human check. Mechanism in the quote: lower wind speed. Author frames the measurements as high-wind / dust events (abstract, conclusions), hence hazard_type; no significance test reported. The paper's conclusion restates this as a 20% decrease in dust emissions.

yield was reduced in AC by −22% compared to rainfed conditions

context.practice_as_described: 25-year-old walnut-based alley cropping: hybrid walnut trees (Juglans regia x nigra) planted in 1995 on east-west tree lines separating cropped alleys, stand density halved by selective thinning in 2004; winter pea grown in the alleys with no fertilizer and one fungicide, hand weeding; compared with an agricultural control (full sun) in the northern part of the same parcel
context.note: One season (2018-2019), one site; AF and agricultural control (AC) are not randomised within the parcel (authors note this limitation, p3) though soil texture is homogeneous. Quadrats at 3.5 m north and south of the tree lines (32 AF, 8 AC). Spring drought was IMPOSED by mobile rainout shelters (135 mm excluded, April to end of May, rain-excluded = EXC vs rainfed = CTL); the hazard is experimental, the practice is the real walnut system. Buffering of the drought IMPACT, not a yield advantage over full sun (see blan22_2: AF still yields less than AC under drought). The light x rainfall interaction on grain yield is p < .001. The relative gain within AF partly reflects how depressed AF yields were in the rainfed arm.

units.citation: Asare et al. (2018). On-farm cocoa yields increase with canopy cover of shade trees in two agro-ecological zones in Ghana. Climate and Development.
units.quote:
With the present study, which
shows a positive correlation between shade cover and
yield at ﬁeld level, we have evidence to support that
larger CC from shade trees results in increasing yields.
Smaller yields under shade trees thus seem to be offset
by positive effects of shade on the rest of the ﬁeld.
Hence, compared to farms with no shade trees, yields at
34% CC would be approximately doubled (Figure 2).

relationship.outcome_raw: whole-farm dry cocoa bean yield against canopy cover of upper-canopy shade trees, linear mixed model controlling district, farm size, previous land use, training and fertilizer; the model predicts roughly a doubling from no shade trees to the top of the observed cover range; mechanism per the authors: lower yields directly under shade trees are offset by positive shade effects across the rest of the field, plausibly natural soil-fertility maintenance and non-chemical pest and disease control under low-input management

context.practice_as_described: cocoa farms of 8-28-year-old cocoa trees with a variable number of upper-canopy shade trees (2.1 to 66.7 trees per ha, canopy cover 1.0% to 34% of farm area), 96% of the shade trees from natural regeneration, under smallholder low-input management with variable fertilizer, fungicide and insecticide use
context.note: 86 farm plots, 2009-2013 yields from farm records confirmed by Cocoa Purchasing records. CC effect gamma = 0.07, p < 0.0001 on cube-root yield (p6). 'Approximately doubled' is a model prediction with no baseline yield stated in the sentence: fold-change sets direction only (Pete 2026-10-20), so no strength. Farm size is confounded with CC (smaller farms have more cover, p6). Dose-response within the observed range only (CC up to about 30-34%); authors do not claim the rise continues beyond it. Cocoa-specific (claim_scope crop_specific, re-included for F5 shaded perennials per crop_scope_policy). The earlier plot-level study by the same authors (Asare et al. 2017) found lower yields directly under shade trees than in full sun - cited, not extracted.

relationship.outcome_raw: PVINR of 4 m alley cropping vs the short-cycle bush fallow control, low population density (no yield penalty on fallow), base-case discount rate

context.practice_as_described: continuous-cultivation maize alley cropping with Leucaena leucocephala hedgerows planted at 4 m interhedgerow spacing, hedgerows periodically pruned (about 20% of the land occupied by trees per the authors)
context.note: Comparator = the authors' control, traditional bush fallow with 3-year cropping in a 6-year cycle (50% farming intensity). Other arms in the same model: no-till with herbicide, and 3-year cropping in a 12-year cycle bush fallow. Simulation: SCUAF (simplified USLE) erosion over a 20-year horizon for a sandy Oxic Paleustalf, 7% slope, seeded with IITA Ibadan plot erosion rates (Kang and Ghuman 1989; Sabel-Koschella et al. 1984); maize yield from Lal (1981) yield-cumulative-soil-loss function. Mechanism: hedgerows lower erosion through a tree proportionality factor in SCUAF (degree to which erosion is controlled by the tree component); lower cumulative soil loss sustains maize yield; pruning raises labour. PVINR = present value of incremental net returns over 20 years vs the 6-year-cycle bush fallow control, 1988 naira (US$1 = N5.00), farmer receives no salvage value (p = 0). Ordinal use only; no currency normalisation. Positive vs the control but LOWER than the long 12-year-cycle bush fallow: where land is abundant, long fallow is the most profitable system; labour costs would need to fall by at least 10% (4 m) for alley cropping to compete (p360).

context.practice_as_described: Coffea arabica cv. Catuai planted 1995 at 3 x 1 m on a smallholder farm in Araponga (Zona da Mata, Minas Gerais); the farmer planted 25 trees between the coffee rows the same year, thinned in 1998 to favour the deciduous Erythrina verna; trees pruned annually. Both shaded and unshaded areas share the same management: manual weed control without soil exposure, legumes (Calopogonium, perennial soybean) in the herbaceous stratum, small doses of lime and NPK, no pesticides. Shaded vs unshaded areas differ only by the presence of the trees (same slope position).
context.note: Paired comparison on ONE farm, one shaded and one unshaded 10 x 10 m area, one pluviometer and one sensor set per area, Aug 2009 - Jun 2010; no replication and no significance testing (case study). Altitude 918 m, mean annual temperature 18 C, 1200-1800 mm rainfall. framing=loss: the sentence states the practice-ABSENT side (unshaded) relative to the shaded side, so direction is recorded as measured (wetter without trees) and the engine flips it to the practice-present frame (shade = drier, a harm finding). Kept narrative so the with/without contrast fields cannot be misread under the flip; values 0.39 (unshaded) and 0.19 (shaded) are in outcome_raw. Layer II = 20-40 cm. AWCI = (moisture - PWP)/(FC - PWP); 0.5 is the authors' coffee water-stress reference. Mechanism: lower internal rainfall plus deeper coffee rooting promoted by the drier surface layer under shade (p13).
